qs.q: Which of the following dermatophyte genera is distinguished by producing only macroconidia and lacking microconidia entirely?
qs.e: Epidermophyton floccosum produces only macroconidia and lacks microconidia, which serves as a key distinguishing laboratory feature. Other dermatophytes produce both forms.

qs.q: Which dermatophyte genus is characterized by numerous, thick-walled, rough, spindle-shaped, multicellular macroconidia and rare microconidia?
qs.e: Microsporum species produce numerous thick-walled, rough, spindle-shaped macroconidia with rare microconidia. Epidermophyton features club-shaped macroconidia and no microconidia, while Trichophyton has abundant microconidia.
qs.s: Medical Fungi: Classification, Morphology, Reproduction & Spores: MCQs

qs.q: A dermatologist examines a skin scraping and identifies numerous, smooth-walled, club-shaped macroconidia in clusters, with no microconidia present. Which dermatophyte genus is this?
qs.e: Epidermophyton is characterized by numerous, smooth-walled, club-shaped macroconidia in clusters and the absence of microconidia. Microsporum has rough, spindle-shaped macroconidia, and Trichophyton has rare, pencil-shaped macroconidia.
qs.s: Medical Fungi: Classification, Morphology, Reproduction & Spores: MCQs

qs.q: While examining a macroscopic fungal colony from a dermatophyte culture under low magnification, a student notes a dense, interwoven network of branching filaments. Which term correctly identifies an individual microscopic component of this network?
qs.e: A mycelium is macroscopic and composed of a mass of individual filamentous tubes known as hyphae. Yeasts, spores, and fruiting bodies represent different morphological structures rather than the basic filamentous building block.
qs.s: Medical Fungi: Classification, Morphology, Reproduction & Spores: MCQs

qs.q: Which dermatophyte genus is characterized by rare, thin-walled, smooth, pencil-shaped macroconidia and abundant microconidia?
qs.e: Trichophyton has rare, pencil-shaped macroconidia and abundant microconidia. Microsporum has numerous, rough, spindle-shaped macroconidia, and Epidermophyton has club-shaped macroconidia and no microconidia.
qs.s: Medical Fungi: Classification, Morphology, Reproduction & Spores: MCQs

qs.q: A farmer presents with an inflamed, boggy scalp lesion known as a kerion following a dermatophyte infection. What pathological process underlies this clinical presentation?
o: Direct toxic mycotoxin destruction of epidermal cells
A strong host immune reaction to the dermatophyte
Complete suppression of local T-lymphocyte responses
Unchecked intravascular proliferation of dimorphic hyphae
qs.e: A kerion is an inflamed, boggy scalp lesion resulting from a strong immune reaction to a dermatophyte. It is an exaggerated local tissue response rather than direct toxin-mediated necrosis.
qs.s: Mycoses: Fungal Pathogenesis, Virulence & Host Immune Defense: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with a dermatophyte infection develops fungus-free skin lesions on a distant part of their body. What is the immunological term for this phenomenon?
qs.e: An 'id reaction' describes fungus-free skin lesions appearing elsewhere on the body due to hypersensitivity to circulating fungal antigens. Granulomas represent delayed Type IV hypersensitivity to intracellular fungi, not distant sterile lesions.
qs.s: Mycoses: Fungal Pathogenesis, Virulence & Host Immune Defense: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following characteristics accurately differentiates dermatophytes of the genus Microsporum from Epidermophyton?
o: A. Microsporum infects hair and skin with many rough macroconidia, while Epidermophyton infects skin and nails with smooth club‑shaped macroconidia.
B. Microsporum produces many microconidia and commonly affects children, whereas Epidermophyton lacks microconidia and mainly affects adults.
D. Microsporum primarily targets nails, whereas Epidermophyton spares nails and targets hair follicles.
C. Microsporum is a geophilic species with no anthropophilic forms, whereas Epidermophyton is transmitted by domestic animals.
qs.e: Microsporum characteristically infects hair and skin with numerous thick-walled, rough, spindle-shaped macroconidia, while Epidermophyton infects skin and nails with numerous smooth, club-shaped macroconidia in clusters and lacks microconidia. Epidermophyton affects adults mainly, whereas Microsporum predominantly affects children.
qs.s: Mycoses: Superficial, Cutaneous & Systemic Fungal Infections: MCQs

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Dermatophytes are fungi that invade keratinised skin, hair and nails, causing tinea infections. They trigger a cellular immune response and can present with characteristic ring‑shaped lesions.

sections.p: Dermatophytes are filamentous fungi that digest keratin. They are classified into three genera—Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton—each with distinct epidemiology.
b: Spread by direct contact or fomites

sections.p: They produce hyaline, septate hyphae and macroconidia whose shape helps species identification.
b: Macroconidia: club‑shaped in Microsporum, spindle‑shaped in Trichophyton
Require keratin for growth; cannot invade deep tissue

sections.p: Spores are shed from infected skin, hair or nails and survive on surfaces for months, allowing spread in households, schools and communal showers.
b: Animal reservoirs (e.g., cats, dogs) for zoophilic species

sections.p: Dermatophytes cause tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea pedis, tinea unguium and tinea capitis, each defined by location and clinical pattern.
b: Tinea capitis: scaly, alopecic patches, common in children
Tinea unguium: nail thickening, subungual debris
Inflammatory variants (e.g., erythema migrans‑like) may mimic bacterial infection

sections.p: Clinical appearance guides initial suspicion; laboratory confirmation uses microscopy and culture, but rapid point‑of‑care tests are useful when resources are limited.
b: Wood's lamp: bright fluorescence in Microsporum infections

t.b: Does the sample contain fungal hyphae? Positive confirms dermatophyte infection.
What species is present? Species guides epidemiology and treatment duration.
Is there fluorescence? Positive suggests Microsporum spp.; negative does not rule out infection.

sections.p: First‑line therapy is topical azoles for limited disease; oral agents are required for scalp, nail or extensive infection. Education reduces reinfection.
b: Topical terbinafine or azoles: inhibit ergosterol synthesis, good for tinea corporis/cruris/pedis
Oral terbinafine or itraconazole: preferred for tinea capitis and onychomycosis; avoid griseofulvin in hepatic disease
Keep skin dry, avoid sharing towels, treat pets if zoonotic source

sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, diagnostic steps, and rationale for drug choice.
b: Ring‑shaped, scaly plaque with central clearing → tinea corporis
Hair loss with black dot patches in a child → tinea capitis, confirm with KOH
Nail dystrophy without trauma → consider tinea unguium; culture if available

whenToSeekHelp: Systemic symptoms (fever, chills) with extensive skin involvement
Immunocompromised patient with widespread dermatophyte infection

faq.q: Why do dermatophytes only affect skin, hair and nails?
faq.a: They produce keratinases that digest keratin, the main protein in these tissues, but lack enzymes to invade deeper layers.

faq.q: Can a bacterial infection look like a dermatophyte infection?
faq.a: Yes, erythematous, scaly lesions can mimic cellulitis; KOH microscopy helps differentiate.

faq.q: What if culture facilities are unavailable?
faq.a: A positive KOH exam plus typical clinical features is sufficient to start treatment.
